Warning Signs After Orthopedic Surgery

This document describes warning signs that should prompt immediate medical attention after orthopedic surgery. Recognizing these signs early can prevent serious complications. Keep this document accessible throughout your recovery.

Signs of Wound Infection:
Contact your surgeon's office immediately or go to the emergency room if you notice any of the following at the surgical site: increasing redness or warmth spreading around the incision, purulent (pus-like) drainage from the wound, an unpleasant odor from the wound site, the wound edges separating or opening, or fever above 101°F combined with worsening local symptoms. Early treatment of surgical site infection is essential to prevent deeper joint infection.

Signs of Deep Joint Infection (Periprosthetic Infection):
Deep infection involving the joint implant is a serious complication. Warning signs include severe and worsening pain in the joint that was improving previously, fever above 101°F, chills and night sweats, significant swelling of the joint with no improvement over several days, and redness extending well beyond the incision area. Deep infections require urgent evaluation and may require surgical intervention.

Signs of Blood Clot (Deep Vein Thrombosis — DVT):
Blood clots in the leg veins can form after joint replacement surgery. Symptoms include calf pain or tenderness, swelling in the lower leg or ankle, warmth or redness in the calf, and a feeling of heaviness in the leg. Note: Some leg swelling is normal after surgery, but sudden or significant worsening should be evaluated.

Signs of Pulmonary Embolism (Blood Clot in the Lung):
A pulmonary embolism is a life-threatening emergency. Call 911 immediately if you experience sudden shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, chest pain that worsens with breathing, rapid heart rate, coughing up blood, or lightheadedness or fainting. These symptoms require immediate emergency care.

Signs of Nerve or Vascular Injury:
Though uncommon, nerve or vascular complications can occur. Contact your surgeon promptly if you experience numbness or tingling in the leg or foot that is worsening or new, significant weakness of the foot or ankle (foot drop), pallor (paleness) or coldness of the foot compared to the other side, or severe unrelenting burning or shooting pain.

Falls and Trauma:
If you fall or sustain any trauma to the operative leg, contact your surgeon's office for evaluation even if you do not feel immediate pain. A fall may damage the implant or surrounding tissues and requires professional assessment.

Medication-Related Warning Signs:
If you are taking blood thinners (anticoagulants), seek immediate attention for unusual or excessive bleeding such as: bleeding from cuts that will not stop within 10–15 minutes, blood in urine (pink or red urine), blood in stool (black or tarry stool), coughing or vomiting blood, or excessive bruising.

General Emergency Guidance:
When in doubt, seek medical attention. It is always better to have a symptom evaluated and be reassured than to delay care for a serious complication. Keep the contact number for your surgical team and the nearest emergency room readily available.
